venerate

/VEN-uh-rayt/ - the stress falls on VEN · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Venerate means to regard with deep respect — reverence so complete it borders on worship.

Apprentice stonemasons at the cathedral are taught to venerate the medieval builders, reading their unsigned chisel marks like the signatures of old masters.

Example

In the temple garden, the oldest maple is venerated outright: gardeners bow to it before pruning, visitors lower their voices beneath it, and its fallen leaves are gathered up like relics.

Notice what separates this from ordinary admiration: the bowing, the hushed voices, the relic-treatment. To venerate is to respect something so deeply that the respect takes on the gestures of worship — a reverence usually reserved for great age, sanctity, or long tradition.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

revere: To revere is to hold in deep, awed respect — the feeling itself, wherever it lands. Venerate adds ritual and age to the awe: what is venerated is usually old or sacred, and the respect shows up in gestures — bowing, preserving, hushing — not just in feeling.

idolize: To idolize is to adore so blindly that flaws stop registering — a fan's worship of a pop star. Venerate is steadier and more clear-eyed: it honors proven worth, usually long-proven, and keeps its dignity where idolizing loses it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

scorn: to treat as beneath respect

desecrate: to treat something sacred with violent disrespect

Where it sits · how deep the reverence runs

respect → venerate → worship

respect vs. venerate: Respect is milder than venerate: you respect a fair referee and think no more of it, while venerating adds awe and ritual — a reverence that bows.

worship vs. venerate: Worship is stronger than venerate: veneration stops just short of the altar, while worship crosses over and treats its object as divine.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — vener: love, reverent awe (Latin venus, veneris)

Suffix — -ate: verb ending: to act, to make

Put it together: Vener- (love, reverent awe — the stem of Venus, the Roman goddess of love) + -ate (verb ending) = to treat with loving awe. Latin venerari meant to worship at a shrine; English kept the posture but widened the shrine, so elders, founders, and old traditions can all be venerated now. The same stem survives in venerable — worthy of veneration, usually by having outlasted everyone else.

Use the root in a new word: venial: The abbey's old rulebook sorts every fault a monk could commit into mortal and venial, and spends a full chapter on which is which.

Root Check

Word Choice

solemn / reverent

Venerate is the strongest respect word you can use without claiming religion outright: it implies age, ritual, and a touch of awe. Revere runs close but stays inward — a feeling; veneration shows. Exalt, taught earlier in this unit, praises upward — it raises its subject with words — while venerate bows before a subject already high. Save it for elders, founders, and traditions; venerating a gadget is a joke on the speaker.
